title: High-speed Java
lead: This project is first of all a Java demo, and this page shows the Java techniques behind its speed: plain numeric code, the Vector API, GPU kernels with TornadoVM and virtual threads. Each comes with an excerpt of the real code and a measured speed-up, compared with C++ where measured. Java in and near the browser, with TeaVM and Hilla, has a chapter of its own.
toc.outlook: Outlook: Valhalla and the final Vector API
sec.overview.title: Java in this project
sec.overview.p1: Four Java techniques in this project have a measured effect on speed. Plain Java without an object per move runs the classical search at about {n:1.6} million nodes per second on one core. The {term:vector-api|Vector API} makes the {term:forward-pass|forward pass} of the network about 15 times faster than scalar Java. {term:tornadovm|TornadoVM} moves it to the GPU, and {term:virtual-thread|virtual threads} feed that GPU during training. How the Java search runs in the browser is the subject of {sec:java-web/overview|Java in the browser}.
sec.overview.p2: The figure puts the forward pass of the {term:small-large|SMALL} network on one log axis. As a rough rule from these measurements: SIMD gives a factor of about 15, and a GPU with large batches another factor of about 37. At batch 1 the GPU is slower than one CPU thread for this network. Only the three Mac rows come from one run; the others come from other machines and runs, so read them as orders of magnitude, not as exact ratios. In the classical search, which the figure does not show, incremental updates in plain Java gave about 30 %.
sec.overview.p3: A note on measuring Java: the {term:jit|JIT compiler} turns hot bytecode into machine code only while the program runs, so the first calls are slower. The project's benchmarks therefore warm up before they measure; the C++ comparison, for example, runs the JIT and the TornadoVM compilation in an untimed warm-up. The JIT even shows in results: the Vector API network gave last-digit differences between its first and later calls on the same input, probably interpreted code against compiled code.
sec.plain-java.title: Fast plain Java
sec.plain-java.p1: Java gets fast when the hot path allocates nothing. A move is an `int`, `from | (to << 8)`, not an object. The board is a `byte[]` with the owner of each cell, plus a piece list per player. The search plays and takes back moves on one mutable position ({term:make-unmake|make/unmake}) and keeps the undo data in parallel primitive arrays. Move generation fills the caller's array and returns the count. The jump search keeps its visited set of {n:121} cells in two `long` values, so it stays in registers ({src:engine/src/main/java/sternhalma/engine/Position.java}).
sec.plain-java.p2: The same idea helped the evaluation. About two thirds of a leaf evaluation went into one {term:feature}, the best one-move gain. An incremental version updates its sums in make and unmake instead of recomputing them ({src:search/src/main/java/sternhalma/search/IncrementalLinear.java}). With identical search trees, the search became about 30 % faster in nodes per second, and self-play played about {n:1.45} times as many games per CPU second. The machine was busy with other jobs during these runs, so the numbers are indicative. They come from another run than the {n:1.6} million nodes per second above, so the two numbers do not form a before and after.
sec.plain-java.p3: A faithful C++ port, with the same algorithms and move order and no extra optimisation, runs the same search {n:1.5} to {n:1.7} times as fast: about {n:2.6} against {n:1.6} million nodes per CPU second on one core of an Apple M3 Max, in one native run. That C++ build keeps {term:bounds-check|bounds checks} on, as Java always does; they cost C++ 11 to 13 %. The JVM also starts slower: about {n:0.85} s against {n:0.26} s to the end of a one-position search ({term:cold-start|cold start}).
sec.vector-api.title: SIMD with the Vector API
sec.vector-api.p1: {term:simd|SIMD} means that one CPU instruction works on several numbers at once: 4 floats with NEON on the Mac, 8 with AVX2 and 16 with AVX-512, measured on an Intel Xeon. The {term:vector-api|Vector API} gives plain Java access to these instructions. A {term:vector-species|species} fixes the vector width. The project picks it once in a `static final` field, because the JIT compiles vector code only for a constant species. The inner loop of the convolution loads 2 weight vectors, broadcasts 4 input cells and runs 8 {term:fma|fused multiply-adds} into 8 accumulators.
sec.vector-api.p2: On one M3 Max core this is about 15 times faster than the scalar Java reference. The Mac has only 4 {term:lane|lanes}, so the lanes alone give at most 4 products per instruction. The rest comes from the shape of the loop, where 4 cells share each weight load, and from the reference, which sums in `double` in a fixed order; no measurement splits the factor. Against hand-written C++ SIMD on the Mac, C++ is about 12 % ahead for the {term:small-large|LARGE} network at batch 256. Without FMA in C++ both are about equal; the Java Vector API always uses FMA. A tile with 16 {term:accumulator|accumulators} was 4 times slower, probably because HotSpot did not keep 16 vectors in registers.
sec.vector-api.p3: The API is still an {term:incubator-module|incubator module}: the build adds `--add-modules jdk.incubator.vector`, and the JVM prints a warning at start. Without the module, the code falls back to the scalar network ({src:nn/src/main/java/sternhalma/nn/Networks.java}). One story from the cloud: in the first run on an AVX-512 machine, C++ was about 5 times slower than Java. The cause was a defect of the C++ port, with bounds checks and a stack copy in the inner loop. After the fix, C++ was about {n:1.3} times faster; the source rates that figure as indicative.
sec.auto-vectorization.title: Auto-vectorization: currently not used in the code
sec.auto-vectorization.p1: With {term:auto-vectorization|auto-vectorization}, the JIT compiler turns an ordinary loop over arrays into SIMD instructions by itself. HotSpot's C2 compiler does this in a pass called {term:superword|SuperWord}, and the pass is on by default in the JDK 25 that the project uses. C2 may therefore vectorize simple scalar loops here, such as the ReLU of the reference path. No code relies on it, no benchmark measures it, and no build file sets a related flag. Whether C2 vectorizes any loop of this project was not checked.
sec.auto-vectorization.p2: The fast path is written with the Vector API instead, because C2 keeps the order of floating-point sums: a different order rounds differently. An OpenJDK developer wrote in 2024 that such sums do vectorize on x64 but run no faster than scalar code, and that the ARM backend, which the Mac uses, does not vectorize them at all. On the Mac, a dot product like the hex convolution therefore stays scalar; on x64, vectorizing it would gain nothing. The scalar reference even sums in `double` in a fixed order on purpose: it is the oracle that the fast versions are tested against ({src:nn/src/main/java/sternhalma/nn/ReferenceOps.java}). On the C++ side, GCC's auto-vectorizer does not touch the corresponding loop either; that loop is vectorized by hand.
sec.tornadovm.title: GPU kernels with TornadoVM
sec.tornadovm.p1: A GPU runs thousands of small {term:gpu-thread|GPU threads} at once. A GPU thread is not a `java.lang.Thread`: it runs the body of a parallel loop for one index. A {term:kernel} is that body, compiled for the GPU, and a {term:kernel-launch|launch} is the command of the host to start one kernel. The hardware runs 32 GPU threads together as a {term:warp}; Apple calls this group a SIMD-group. Warps run on the {term:sm|SMs} of an NVIDIA GPU, 40 on a Tesla T4; the Apple M3 Max has 40 GPU cores instead. Each SM has its own registers and a small, fast memory, split between the {term:l1-cache|L1 cache} and the {term:shared-memory|shared memory} of a {term:work-group|work group}. One {term:l2-cache|L2 cache} serves all SMs.
sec.tornadovm.p2: Where the data lives depends on the machine. A discrete NVIDIA card has its own {term:device-memory|device memory}: the T4 has 16 GB at about 300 GB/s, but its link to the host, {term:pcie|PCI Express}, carries 16 GB/s in each direction. A current card such as the GeForce RTX 5090 reads its own memory at about 1,800 GB/s and the host at most at 64 GB/s, so local data is much faster there too. Apple Silicon has {term:unified-memory|unified memory}: CPU and GPU share one memory, 400 GB/s on the M3 Max, with no link in between. TornadoVM 7.3.1 still copies from the Java arrays into its own Metal buffers in that memory, for less than 0.01 ms per call.
sec.tornadovm.p3: {term:tornadovm|TornadoVM} compiles Java methods into kernels at run time: into Metal Shading Language on the Mac, and into CUDA C, which NVIDIA's run-time compiler NVRTC translates, on Linux. The two outer loops of the convolution carry `@Parallel`, and TornadoVM turns them into the grid of GPU threads, one per output value. A {term:task-graph|task graph} says what to copy and what to run: the weights go to the GPU once and stay there, the inputs go on every call. One forward pass launches 11 kernels for the SMALL network and 15 for LARGE.
sec.tornadovm.p4: Every call has a large fixed cost. On the Mac a SMALL call with one position takes about 0.5 ms. A single convolution kernel runs for only 0.03 to 0.2 ms of that, yet a call with just this one kernel already takes about 0.3 ms. The rest is the price of the call itself: the launches, the work of the runtime, the wait for the result, and a GPU that one position cannot fill. The copies are not the main cost: in a hand-written C++ backend on the T4 they take at most 11 % of the device time. The GPU is full from about 256 positions per call, where SMALL reaches 94 % of its best rate. One position then costs about 57 times less than at batch 1 for SMALL on the Mac, and 17 to 18 times less on the T4. At batch 1, one CPU thread with the Vector API is faster than the GPU for SMALL; for LARGE the GPU wins already there.
sec.tornadovm.p5: The project therefore uses {term:batching} across games, not inside one search. In self-play, hundreds of games run as virtual threads. Each asks for one position and blocks, and one {term:device-thread|device thread} computes the positions of many games in one call. A batch leaves when it is full, after 250 µs of quiet while the GPU is idle, or after 20 ms at the latest. Each game keeps its search at batch 1 and so its playing strength. Only the WebGPU engine in the browser batches inside one search tree, with 4 or 8 leaves, because more leaves cost strength. At batch 256 the GPU of the M3 Max computes about {n:110000} SMALL evaluations per second, about 37 times one Vector API thread; on the T4, TornadoVM and hand-written CUDA both reach about {n:85000}.
sec.tornadovm.p6: A new TornadoVM process on the T4 needs 3 to {n:4.4} s to its first result, C++ CUDA about {n:0.2} s. The batch size is compiled into the kernel, so the project rounds batches up to a power of two, one compiled plan per {term:bucket}, and a {term:kernel-choice-rule|kernel-choice rule} picks the kernel per bucket. A kernel has no {term:bounds-check|bounds checks}: a read past the end returns 0. Metal's `tanh` returns 0 or NaN for large arguments. Unsupported Java fails with an `Error`, not an exception. One Java source serves Metal and CUDA: {n:1372} non-comment lines of code against {n:1714} for the two C++ backends.
sec.outlook.title: Outlook: Valhalla and the final Vector API
sec.outlook.p1: Two OpenJDK developments would change this code. The Vector API is in its twelfth incubation, JEP 537, delivered in JDK 27. The JEP says it will incubate until the necessary features of Project Valhalla become available as preview features. JEP 401, value objects, is targeted to JDK 28 as a preview; JDK 28 is scheduled for general availability in March 2027. As of 21 November 2026, no Vector API JEP is listed for JDK 28. The project compiles with `--release 25` and uses none of this.
sec.outlook.p2: Instances of a {term:value-class|value class} are immutable and have no identity. In exchange, a JVM can store them flat in arrays and fields instead of as separate objects on the heap. The example in JEP 401 is the declaration `value record Point(int x, int y)`. JEP 537 expects the vector classes, such as `FloatVector`, to become value classes.
sec.outlook.p3: The block below is an illustration, not code of this project; it was neither compiled nor measured. It writes `Move` as a value record instead of a packed `int`. The vector loop would look almost the same; the incubator flag and its warning would go away. Whether a JVM would really flatten `Move[]`, and how fast that would be, is open: JEP 401 says that a JVM can do it, not that it will.
sec.more.title: Also in the code
sec.more.p1: {term:virtual-thread|Virtual threads} feed the GPU during self-play. Each game runs as a virtual thread, and one {term:device-thread|device thread} collects their positions and calls the GPU. A first version used a semaphore over 256 platform threads and reached {n:29000} to {n:46000} evaluations per second, against {n:57000} to {n:82000} with virtual threads, measured minutes apart: roughly {n:1.8} times. On a T4, 512 games on 4 {term:carrier-thread|carrier threads} kept the device thread busy 99 % of the time. One pitfall: a virtual thread has no CPU time of its own.
sec.more.p2: The {term:ffm-api|Foreign Function & Memory API} works behind TornadoVM. Its arrays are off-heap memory segments, and the project copies into them with `MemorySegment.copy` ({src:nn-tornado/src/main/java/sternhalma/tornado/OpsCopy.java}). TornadoVM's CUDA backend calls the driver through `java.lang.foreign`; the project calls no native code of its own. Checked and not in use: GraalVM native image and Gradle toolchains. Still open: `Long.expand` and `Long.compress` give Java the bit instructions PDEP and PEXT, which a bitboard move generator could use; their speed is not measured yet.

fig.javaspeed.desc: A dot chart on a logarithmic axis, in evaluations per second of the SMALL network. The first group has three rows from one run on an Apple M3 Max: scalar Java at batch 1, the Vector API on one thread and TornadoVM on the GPU, both at batch 256. The second group has rows from other machines: the Vector API with AVX-512, TornadoVM and C++ CUDA on a Tesla T4, and scalar Java via TeaVM and C++ WebAssembly in the browser.

fig.javaplain.title: The same code with objects and with primitives
fig.javaplain.desc: Two lanes side by side in three views. The lane with objects is a comparison and is not in the code; the lane with primitives is what the project does. View move: one move as an object with header and reference against one int, and the memory of 67 moves. View undo: three objects on a stack against four parallel arrays with one slot per ply. View evaluation: all 20 pieces read again against one sum updated per move.
fig.javaplain.view.label: Show
fig.javaplain.pick.label: Pick a move
fig.javaplain.caption: The lanes with objects are a comparison; that code is not in the project. Sizes were measured on the project's JVM (OpenJDK 25, default settings); the memory map shows the smallest possible layout. A cache line has 128 bytes on the Apple M3 Max. The position is the mid-game example of the alpha-beta figure, with 67 legal moves. The evaluation view shows one of several terms.
fig.javaplain.mem.objects.desc: Memory map: an array of {n} references and {n} objects, {bytes} bytes, at least {lines} cache lines. The selected move is one reference and one object.
fig.javaplain.mem.primitives.desc: Memory map: the start of one int buffer, {n} moves in {bytes} bytes, at least {lines} cache lines. The selected move is one word.
fig.javaplain.narr.move: Move {k} is {move}. As an int it is one word in a buffer that already exists. As an object it is a reference plus an object with a header.
fig.javaplain.undo.table.caption: Four arrays, one slot per ply. A make writes the slots of the current ply.
fig.javaplain.narr.undo.root: The position at ply {ply}. Nothing is saved yet.
fig.javaplain.narr.undo.make: Make {move} saves four values in slot {ply}: 20 bytes, no new object. The other way creates an object of 32 bytes.
fig.javaplain.narr.undo.unmake: Unmake reads slot {ply} back. The values stay in the arrays; the object of the other way becomes garbage.
fig.javaplain.narr.undo.reuse: Make {move} overwrites slot {ply}. The other way creates a third object.
fig.javaplain.narr.undo.done: Back at the root. Three makes: no allocation, against three objects (96 bytes) for the garbage collector. A search does this at every node.
fig.javaplain.narr.eval.root: At the root the distance sums are 70 for A and 66 for B.
fig.javaplain.narr.eval.make: {move} moves one piece from distance {df} to {dt}. The update changes one sum by the difference and saves the old sums in a frame that already exists.
fig.javaplain.narr.eval.leaf: At a leaf the search needs the evaluation. The full way reads 20 pieces. The incremental way already has the sums; it changed one of them for {move}.
fig.javaplain.narr.eval.unmake: Unmake copies the saved frame back.
fig.javaplain.narr.eval.done: Two evaluations: 40 pieces read against 3 pieces updated.

fig.simd.title: One pass of the convolution loop with the Vector API
fig.simd.desc: A grid of 4 board cells by 32 output channels, one box per product. A slider sets the lanes per register to 1, 4, 8 or 16; the same loop body then covers a larger part of the row. A stepper walks the loop body: 2 weight loads, 4 broadcasts, 8 fused multiply-adds, then the stores. A number line sets the lane count beside the measured speed-up of about 15 times scalar Java on a machine with 4 lanes.
fig.simd.lanes.label: Lanes per register
fig.simd.pre.label: Machine
fig.simd.narr.idle: The grid shows {cells} board cells by the {channels} output channels of the SMALL network, for one input channel of one cell of the neighbourhood. Each box is one product. Step through the loop.
fig.simd.narr.load: Two loads fill w0 and w1 with the weights of the first tile, one weight per lane.
fig.simd.narr.bcast: Four broadcasts copy the input value of each of the 4 cells into every lane of v0 to v3.
fig.simd.narr.fma: One FMA adds {w} × {v} to {acc}: one instruction for every lane of the register, here {lanes}. Each of the 8 FMAs has its own accumulator.
fig.simd.narr.done: One pass is done: {fmas} FMAs gave {products} products. The pass repeats {repeats} times for these 4 cells (7 cells of the hex neighbourhood × 32 input channels). Then {stores} stores write the 8 accumulators; the next tile and the next 4 cells follow.
fig.simd.grid.desc: Grid of 4 board cells by 32 output channels, one box per product. Tiles: {tiles}, each 2 registers; lanes per register: {lanes}. The stepper fills the first tile.
fig.simd.meas.desc: Number line. Products per instruction at the chosen width: {lanes}. Measured: 15 to 17 times scalar Java, on a machine with 4 lanes.
fig.simd.meas.measured: Measured: the Vector API is {lo} to {hi} times as fast as scalar Java (M3 Max, 4 lanes, 1 thread).
fig.simd.meas.note.neon: 4 lanes cannot give 15 times. More differs: 4 cells share each weight load, 8 accumulators work side by side, and the scalar reference sums in double in a fixed order. No measurement splits the gain.
fig.simd.meas.note.scalar: 1 lane: one product per instruction. This is the same loop as a thought model; the measured scalar path is other, simpler code.
fig.simd.meas.note.avx2: 8 lanes: twice the products per instruction of the M3. This project did not measure this width against scalar Java.
fig.simd.meas.note.avx512: 16 lanes: one tile covers all 32 channels. This width ran on an AWS Xeon host, but not against scalar Java, so the 15 times does not carry over.
fig.simd.caption: Simplified: one input channel, one cell of the neighbourhood, one block of 4 cells; the residual add and the ReLU of the store are left out. The code is the same at every width, because the lane count is a constant read when the class loads. A tile with 16 accumulators was 4 times slower in a test, probably for lack of registers; the cause was not analysed.
fig.gpu.title: Anatomy of a GPU, from the machine to one thread
fig.gpu.desc: Five zoom levels: the whole machine, the inside of the GPU, one SM or GPU core, one warp, and the kernel grid that TornadoVM launches. A switch chooses an Apple M3 Max, an NVIDIA Tesla T4 or an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090. A stepper follows one call from the Java array to one GPU thread and back. A table compares the three machines.
fig.gpu.caption: The kernel grid counts one convolution of the LARGE network, rounded. The RTX 5090 did not run in this project; its numbers are its specification. A dash or a dashed box means that the maker publishes no value.
fig.gpu.anat.label: GPU anatomy in five levels
fig.gpu.hw.label: Hardware
fig.gpu.stepper.label: Follow one call
fig.gpu.unknown.long: The maker publishes no figures for this part.
fig.gpu.narr.idle: Five levels, from the whole machine down to one GPU thread. Step through one call, or open any part for details.
fig.gpu.narr.host.discrete: The Java program runs on the host CPU. One Java thread, the device thread, makes every GPU call. The arrays (FloatArray, off the heap) lie in host memory.
fig.gpu.narr.host.unified: The Java program runs on the CPU. One Java thread, the device thread, makes every GPU call. The arrays lie in the one memory that CPU and GPU share.
fig.gpu.narr.path.discrete: The input crosses {link} to the memory of the card. The link carries {linkRate}, the memory behind it {memRate}. Still, in this project the copies are a small part of a call (next figure).
fig.gpu.narr.path.unified: No link: CPU and GPU read the same memory ({memRate}). TornadoVM still copies from the Java array to its Metal buffer inside that memory, for less than {copy} per call.
fig.gpu.narr.gpu.discrete: Inside the GPU, the device memory ({mem}) holds the weights, copied once, and the input of this call. One L2 cache ({l2}) serves all {units} SMs, which do the work.
fig.gpu.narr.gpu.unified: Inside the GPU, weights and input lie in the unified memory ({mem}). Apple describes one on-chip cache and publishes no sizes. {units} GPU cores do the work.
fig.gpu.narr.unit.discrete: One SM runs many warps and switches among them. It has its own registers and {l1} of fast memory, split between the L1 cache and the shared memory of its work groups.
fig.gpu.narr.unit.unified: One GPU core. Apple publishes no inner structure. A threadgroup gets up to {tg} of fast threadgroup memory.
fig.gpu.narr.warp: A warp is 32 GPU threads that the hardware runs together. On NVIDIA all 32 execute the same instruction at the same time. Apple calls its group of 32 threads a SIMD-group.
fig.gpu.narr.thread.discrete: One GPU thread runs the kernel body for one index of the parallel loop. It is not a java.lang.Thread. The farther away the memory, the longer a read takes; the ladder shows the order.
fig.gpu.narr.thread.unified: One GPU thread runs the kernel body for one index of the parallel loop. It is not a java.lang.Thread. The ladder has two known rungs: the on-chip cache and the unified memory.
fig.gpu.narr.grid: TornadoVM turns the two @Parallel loops into a grid of GPU threads: about {threads1} for one position, about {threads256} for 256. The fast kernels cut it into work groups of {group} threads, 4 warps.
fig.gpu.narr.back.discrete: The result buffer travels back over the link, and the device thread goes on. Every call pays this round trip and one launch per kernel; the next figure shows what that costs.
fig.gpu.narr.back.unified: The result is copied back into the Java array, inside the same memory, and the device thread goes on. The next figure shows what one call costs.
fig.gpu.part.cpu.what: The JVM runs here. One device thread makes all GPU calls, because the TornadoVM network object is not thread-safe.
fig.gpu.part.cpu.java: Like a single-thread executor in front of a resource that is not thread-safe.
fig.gpu.part.hostmem.what: Ordinary RAM of the host. TornadoVM's FloatArray objects keep their data here, off the Java heap.
fig.gpu.part.hostmem.java: Like a MemorySegment of the FFM API: memory outside the heap that the garbage collector does not move.
fig.gpu.part.link.what: PCI Express between host memory and the card. Much narrower than the memory on either side.
fig.gpu.part.link.java: Like a network hop between two services: all data must cross it, and it is narrower than either side. Unlike a hop, nothing is serialised.
fig.gpu.part.copy.what: TornadoVM 7.3.1 keeps its Metal buffers apart from the Java arrays, so it copies although no link exists. The copy costs less than 0.01 ms per call.
fig.gpu.part.copy.java: Like System.arraycopy into a second buffer in the same heap: cheap, but not free.
fig.gpu.part.devmem.what: The card's own memory. The weights stay here between calls. It is the slowest memory that a GPU thread reads.
fig.gpu.part.devmem.java: Like the local store of a remote service: fast for the service, but the caller reaches it only over the link.
fig.gpu.part.umem.what: One memory pool for CPU and GPU, with no link between them. For a GPU thread it is still the farthest memory.
fig.gpu.part.umem.java: Like two threads that share one heap, not two processes. TornadoVM still copies into buffers of its own.
fig.gpu.part.gpu.what: The whole processor: the SMs or GPU cores and their caches. One forward pass of the network launches 11 (SMALL) or 15 (LARGE) kernels on it.
fig.gpu.part.gpu.java: Like a second machine with thousands of very simple cores, reached through a call rather than a method invocation.
fig.gpu.part.l2.what: One cache for all SMs, in front of the device memory. On the T4 it has 4 MB, and a hit takes about 190 cycles.
fig.gpu.part.l2.java: Like the last-level cache that all cores of a CPU share. The comparison covers its place in the hierarchy, not its size or speed.
fig.gpu.part.cache.what: Apple describes one cache that serves register, threadgroup and buffer data and is assigned as needed. Apple publishes no sizes.
fig.gpu.part.cache.java: Like one memory pool that the runtime splits among its users as needed, instead of fixed parts. Apple gives no further details.
fig.gpu.part.sm.what: Streaming multiprocessor: the unit of an NVIDIA GPU that runs warps. A T4 SM holds up to 32 warps at a time and switches among them.
fig.gpu.part.sm.java: Like a CPU core with very wide hyper-threading. The comparison ends at the warp: its 32 threads share one instruction.
fig.gpu.part.core.what: Apple's unit of the GPU; the M3 Max has 40. Apple publishes no inner structure.
fig.gpu.part.core.java: The nearest counterpart of an NVIDIA SM. That the two match is not confirmed.
fig.gpu.part.l1.what: Fast memory on the SM, split between the L1 cache and the shared memory that the threads of one work group read and write. The tiled kernels of this project load their data here first.
fig.gpu.part.l1.java: Shared memory is like a scratch array that a group of threads fills together, with a barrier before anyone reads it.
fig.gpu.part.tgmem.what: Apple's name for the fast memory of one threadgroup: up to 32 KB, shared by up to 1,024 threads.
fig.gpu.part.tgmem.java: Like a scratch array that a group of threads fills together, with a barrier before anyone reads it.
fig.gpu.part.reg.what: Each GPU thread has registers of its own, the nearest memory. On the T4 one SM has 64K registers of 32 bit for all its threads.
fig.gpu.part.reg.java: Like the local variables that the JIT keeps in CPU registers; here every one of thousands of threads has its own set.
fig.gpu.part.warp.what: 32 GPU threads that run together. An SM holds several warps and switches among them.
fig.gpu.part.warp.java: Like 32 threads that always execute the same line together. A branch that only some take makes the others wait.
fig.gpu.part.simd.what: Apple's name for a warp: a group of 32 threads.
fig.gpu.part.simd.java: The same size as an NVIDIA warp. This figure claims nothing more about it.
fig.gpu.part.simt.what: On NVIDIA all 32 threads of a warp execute the same instruction at the same time. Apple groups 32 threads the same way.
fig.gpu.part.simt.java: Like one Vector API operation on 32 lanes, except that each lane has its own registers and its own loop index.
fig.gpu.part.thread.what: One index of the parallel loop: the kernel body runs once per GPU thread.
fig.gpu.part.thread.java: Not a java.lang.Thread. A TornadoVM kernel cannot create an array of dynamic size, and a kernel that throws fails with an Error.
fig.gpu.part.group.what: The threads that share one block of fast memory and can wait for each other at a barrier. CUDA calls it a thread block, Metal a threadgroup. On NVIDIA all its threads run on one SM.
fig.gpu.part.group.java: Like a small group of threads with a CyclicBarrier and a shared array; its size is fixed at launch.

fig.j5.title: What one GPU call costs, and what batching changes
fig.j5.desc: One forward call of the network on the GPU through TornadoVM, for five measured batch sizes on two machines. A bar splits the call into the work for its positions and the overhead of the call itself. A plot shows the time per position over the batch size, next to one CPU thread. A list shows the steps of one call, and three cards say where the project batches.
fig.j5.machine.label: Machine
fig.j5.net.label: Network
fig.j5.preset.label: Where in the project
fig.j5.batch.label: Positions per call
fig.j5.call.heading: This call
fig.j5.call.aria: Time of this call, split into the work for its positions and the overhead of the call itself
fig.j5.verdict.dominates.head: The call itself is the cost
fig.j5.verdict.dominates.text: The host starts 11 or 15 kernels and waits for the result, all for a few positions. The copy is not the reason.
fig.j5.verdict.mixed.head: Positions share the cost
fig.j5.verdict.mixed.text: The same fixed cost is now shared by more positions. The GPU is not full yet, so larger batches still pay.
fig.j5.verdict.amortized.head: Fixed cost spread thin
fig.j5.verdict.amortized.text: The GPU is full. More positions add almost nothing, and the call gets long: LARGE at 1,024 takes about 48 ms on the Mac.
fig.j5.curve.heading: Price of one position, by batch
fig.j5.plot.title: Time per position over the batch size
fig.j5.plot.desc: The time per position falls steeply up to batch 64 and is nearly flat from 256: {first} at batch 1, {last} at batch 1,024. One CPU thread needs {cpu} per position.
fig.j5.table.caption: Measured batch sizes
fig.j5.phases.heading: Inside one call
fig.j5.phases.execute: TornadoVM reports all of this as one number, execute
fig.j5.split.heading: Measured apart
fig.j5.split.empty: Not measured here. Measured: LARGE on the Mac; batch 1, 256 and 1,024 on the T4.
fig.j5.split.note: TornadoVM cannot split its call. These parts come from a hand-written C++ backend with the same kernels, so its total differs from the call above.
fig.j5.where.heading: Where the project batches, and where not
fig.j5.where.pool.title: Self-play: across games
fig.j5.where.pool.text: {games} games run as virtual threads; each asks for one position and blocks. One device thread computes them together, in {cohorts} cohorts of {batch}. A batch leaves when full, after {quiet} of quiet with the GPU idle, or after {maxWait}.
fig.j5.where.tree.title: Inside one tree: browser only
fig.j5.where.tree.text: The search collects {low} or {high} leaves before it calls the network. That changes the search and costs strength: at 200 simulations, batch 16 loses {lossLow} to {lossHigh} of match score.
fig.j5.where.one.title: One game alone: batch 1
fig.j5.where.one.text: The search of one game stays at batch 1, so it plays as it does on the CPU. On its own it would pay the full price of a call for every position.
fig.j5.caption: Measured: whole forward calls through TornadoVM 7.3.1, on an Apple M3 Max (7 November 2026) and an NVIDIA Tesla T4 (15 November 2026). The Mac was loaded by other jobs, so its numbers are lower bounds. Work and overhead are derived from the largest batch, not measured. The CPU value on the T4 is uncertain.
